title: Blackout Drunk: Why You Black Out and How to Avoid It
excerpt: What being blackout drunk really means, why alcohol stops your brain from saving memories, blacking out vs. passing out, the warning signs, and how to avoid it.
metaDescription: What blackout drunk means, why alcohol stops memory forming, blacking out vs. passing out, when it's dangerous, and simple ways to avoid a blackout.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** being "blackout drunk" means you drank enough, fast enough, that your brain stopped recording new memories while you were still awake and doing things. You weren't unconscious. You talked, walked, texted, maybe danced or argued, and other people may have thought you seemed only a bit drunk. Your brain just didn't save it. A blackout is not a sleep problem or a "bad memory" problem. It's a sign that your blood alcohol got high enough to switch off memory storage, and that is a level where injuries, accidents, and alcohol poisoning become real risks.

**The quick rules:** Blackouts are driven mostly by how *fast* your blood alcohol climbs, so shots, drinking games, chugging, and drinking on an empty stomach are the classic setups. Mixing alcohol with sleep aids, anxiety medicines, or opioids makes them much more likely. If you or a friend can't remember chunks of a night, that's a signal to slow down next time, not just a funny story. And if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, or vomiting while drowsy, that's no longer a blackout question. Call 911.

> **When to see a doctor or get help now.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away if** someone who has been drinking can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has blue or pale lips or skin, is vomiting while confused or drowsy, has a seizure, or has hit their head. **Get medical care the same day if** you lost memory after very few drinks or the memory gap doesn't match what you drank (your drink may have been spiked), you think something happened to you during the gap that you didn't agree to, or you were hurt and don't know how. **Talk to your doctor soon if** blackouts keep happening, you black out even when you try to pace yourself, or you take any prescription medicine that could interact with alcohol.

## What "Blackout Drunk" Actually Means

A blackout is a period of memory loss for things that happened while you were intoxicated. The key detail most people miss: **you were awake for it.** During a blackout you can hold conversations, order drinks, find your way home, send messages, and make decisions. Your brain is still running. It's just not writing anything down.

That's why blackouts are so unsettling the next morning. You might find texts you don't remember sending, a receipt from a place you don't remember going, or a friend telling you about a conversation you have no trace of. Nothing is wrong with your long-term memory of the past. Your memories from last week, from childhood, and from earlier in the evening before the blackout started are all intact. The gap is only for the stretch when your blood alcohol was high enough to block new memories from forming.

People often use "blackout drunk" loosely to mean "very drunk." Medically, it means something specific: drunk enough that memory formation shut down. You can be very drunk without a blackout, and some people black out at levels where they don't look especially drunk to anyone else.

## Blacking Out: The Two Types

Researchers usually describe two kinds of alcohol-related blackout.

| Type | What it's like | Can memories come back? |
|---|---|---|
| **En bloc (complete) blackout** | A solid block of time is simply missing. You remember being at the bar, then the next thing you know it's morning. | Generally no. The memories were never stored, so there's nothing to retrieve. |
| **Fragmentary blackout (brownout or greyout)** | Spotty memory. You remember some moments, but there are holes, and the night feels patchy or out of order. | Sometimes partly. Reminders like photos or a friend's description can bring pieces back. |

Fragmentary blackouts are far more common than complete ones. Many people who say "I don't remember much of last night" are describing a brownout. Complete blackouts tend to happen at higher blood alcohol levels and are a stronger warning sign.

### Blacking out vs. passing out

These get mixed up constantly, and the difference matters for safety.

- **Blacking out** is a memory problem. The person is awake and functioning, sometimes surprisingly well.
- **Passing out** is a consciousness problem. The person has fallen asleep or become unresponsive and is hard to wake.

Someone can black out and then pass out later in the same night. Passing out after heavy drinking is the more immediately dangerous of the two, because the alcohol already in the stomach keeps being absorbed, blood alcohol can keep rising after the person stops drinking, and a person who is deeply asleep may not protect their airway if they vomit.

## Why Alcohol Shuts Down Memory: The Brain Science in Plain Words

Your brain doesn't record memories like a video camera. It builds them in stages. What you're experiencing right now goes into short-term memory first, then a brain region called the **hippocampus** does the work of converting it into a lasting memory you can pull up later. That conversion step is called encoding, and it's the step alcohol breaks.

Here's what's going on at a basic level:

- **Alcohol dampens the brain's "go" signals.** It blocks some of the receptors for glutamate, the main chemical messenger the brain uses to strengthen connections between nerve cells. Strengthening those connections is how memories get laid down. Fewer active receptors means weaker memory building.
- **Alcohol boosts the brain's "stop" signals.** It increases the effect of GABA, the main calming messenger. More GABA activity quiets the hippocampus further.
- **The hippocampus is especially sensitive.** Lab research, including work by NIAAA researcher Aaron White and colleagues, has shown that alcohol disrupts activity in hippocampal cells involved in memory in a dose-dependent way. At high enough levels, the encoding process effectively goes offline.

The result is a strange split. The parts of your brain that let you walk, talk, and respond to people can keep working (badly, but working), while the part that saves those experiences for later has stopped. Short-term memory may even work for a few seconds or minutes, which is why someone in a blackout can follow a conversation and still remember none of it the next day.

This is also why a blackout feels so different from forgetting something normally. With normal forgetting, the memory was stored and you can't find it. With a blackout, the memory was never made.

## What Makes a Blackout More Likely

Blackouts aren't just about the number of drinks. Several factors push the odds up.

### How fast your blood alcohol rises

This is the big one. Research on blackouts consistently points to a **rapid rise in blood alcohol** as a stronger predictor than the total amount drunk over a long night. Drinking the same amount slowly over several hours gives your liver time to clear some of it and keeps your peak level lower. Drinking it fast spikes your level before your body can keep up.

That's why the classic blackout scenarios look alike:

- Shots, especially several in a row
- Drinking games and chugging
- "Pre-gaming" quickly before going out
- Strong mixed drinks where you can't taste the alcohol
- Punch bowls and jungle juice, where nobody knows the strength

### Blood alcohol level

The US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) notes that blackouts, especially complete ones, tend to happen at blood alcohol levels around **0.16% and higher**, which is about twice the US legal driving limit of 0.08%. Fragmentary blackouts can happen lower. These numbers are a rough guide, not a line you can safely drink up to. If you want a sense of how drinks, body weight, and time add up, our [blood alcohol calculator](/never-hungover/blood-alcohol-calculator) shows estimated levels, with the big caveat that real-world numbers vary a lot.

### An empty stomach

Food in your stomach slows the rate at which alcohol reaches your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. Drinking on an empty stomach lets alcohol rush into your bloodstream, which is exactly the fast rise that drives blackouts.

### Body size and sex

People with smaller bodies, and women in general, tend to reach higher blood alcohol levels from the same number of drinks. That's because of differences in body water and, to some degree, in how alcohol is processed. Studies of college drinkers have found women report blackouts at lower drinking levels than men.

### Medications and other drugs

Mixing alcohol with other substances that act on the brain can make blackouts much more likely, even at moderate drinking levels. The most important ones:

- **Benzodiazepines** such as Xanax (alprazolam), Valium (diazepam), and Ativan (lorazepam)
- **Sleep medicines** such as Ambien (zolpidem)
- **Opioid painkillers**
- **Gabapentin and pregabalin**
- **Sedating antihistamines** found in many sleep and allergy products
- **Cannabis**, which also affects memory on its own

Many of these also slow breathing, which makes the combination dangerous in a way that goes well beyond memory loss. If you take any of them, ask your doctor or pharmacist how alcohol fits in. For one example of how a common medicine interacts with alcohol, see our guide to [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol).

### Genetics and personal sensitivity

Some people black out more easily than others, even at similar blood alcohol levels. Twin studies suggest part of this vulnerability is inherited. If you've noticed you lose memory at levels where your friends don't, take that as useful information about your own limits rather than a challenge to keep up.

### Tiredness and dehydration

Being short on sleep or already dehydrated doesn't cause blackouts directly, but it tends to make the effects of alcohol feel stronger and makes it harder to judge how drunk you are. Long days followed by a big night out are a common setup.

## How to Tell If Someone Is in a Blackout

Here's the uncomfortable truth: **you often can't tell.** A person in a blackout may look tipsy, loud, or a bit unsteady, but they can also seem fairly together. They might give sensible answers, remember who you are, and carry on a conversation.

Some hints that a friend may be in a blackout:

- They repeat the same question or story several times within a few minutes
- They don't remember something that happened 10 or 15 minutes ago
- They seem "on autopilot," going through the motions without much awareness
- They've had a lot to drink very quickly

Because you can't reliably spot a blackout from the outside, the safer rule is this: **anyone who has drunk enough to possibly be in a blackout is not in a position to make decisions** about driving, going home with someone, swimming, or anything else with real consequences. Their own "I'm fine" doesn't count, because the part of them that would remember agreeing isn't working.

## Why Blackouts Are Dangerous

The memory gap itself isn't what hurts people. What happens during it can.

- **Injuries.** People in blackouts fall, get into fights, and get into cars. Research on college students has linked blackouts to a higher chance of alcohol-related injuries and emergency room visits.
- **Decisions you wouldn't normally make.** Judgment is impaired while you're still able to act. That combination is the core of why blackouts lead to regretted messages, spending, arguments, and risky situations.
- **Sexual consent.** Someone who is blackout drunk cannot meaningfully consent, and people in blackouts are more vulnerable to assault. If you wake up and believe something happened to you that you didn't agree to, you can get medical care and support. In the US, RAINN's hotline (1-800-656-4673) can connect you with local help.
- **Alcohol poisoning.** The blood alcohol levels that cause blackouts aren't far from the levels where breathing and the gag reflex start to fail. A blackout means you were already in the high-risk zone. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) explains what to watch for and when to call 911.

## Could It Have Been Something Else?

If the memory loss doesn't fit what you drank, take that seriously. Losing hours of memory after one or two drinks is not a normal alcohol blackout.

Possible causes worth ruling out:

- **Drink spiking.** Some drugs used to spike drinks cause memory loss, confusion, and drowsiness that come on quickly. Several of them clear from the body fast, so testing works best within hours to a day or two. If you suspect this, go to an emergency department or urgent care as soon as you can and tell them you think your drink was spiked.
- **A head injury.** A fall or hit to the head can cause confusion and memory gaps. Severe or worsening headache, repeated vomiting, unusual sleepiness, or confusion that doesn't clear as you sober up all need medical attention.
- **Medication interactions.** A new prescription can change how alcohol affects you.
- **A seizure** or other medical event, especially if you woke up somewhere unexpected, bit your tongue, or wet yourself.

## What to Do the Morning After a Blackout

Waking up with gaps is stressful. A few practical steps help.

1. **Check on your safety first.** Are you hurt? Is anything missing? Is there anyone you need to check on, or anyone who might be worried about you?
2. **Look after your body.** Drink water, eat something gentle when you can, and rest. You're likely dealing with a real hangover on top of the anxiety.
3. **Fill in the gaps carefully.** Messages, photos, and trusted friends can help you piece things together. Remember that other people's stories aren't always accurate, and your brain can "fill in" gaps with things that didn't happen.
4. **Expect some anxiety.** Not knowing what you said or did is a direct trigger for "hangxiety," the anxious, dreadful feeling many people get after drinking. Our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) covers why it happens and what helps.
5. **Don't drink to take the edge off.** "Hair of the dog" delays the hangover and adds more alcohol to a body that's still recovering.

If you feel foggy or slow for the rest of the day, that's common after heavy drinking. Our article on [brain fog after drinking](/never-hungover/brain-fog-after-drinking) explains why it happens and how long it usually lasts.

## Does Blacking Out Damage Your Brain?

One blackout doesn't mean you've permanently damaged your brain. Your memory should work normally once you've sobered up, and the gap is simply a stretch of time that was never recorded.

That said, blackouts are a marker of drinking at very high levels, and repeated heavy drinking is linked to longer-term effects on the brain. Research on adolescents and young adults is especially cautious, because the brain is still developing into the mid-20s and some studies suggest heavy drinking during those years may affect memory and thinking. The honest summary: a rare blackout is mainly a short-term safety problem, while frequent blackouts point to a pattern that's worth changing. For a broader look at the research, see our guide to [alcohol and long-term brain health](/never-hungover/alcohol-brain-health-long-term-impact-analysis-2025).

## How Common Are Blackouts?

More common than most people assume. Surveys of college students in the US have found that around half of students who drink report having had at least one blackout. Blackouts are not limited to students, though. Plenty of adults have had one at a wedding, a work event, or a birthday where the drinks came faster than usual.

Being common doesn't make them harmless. It mostly reflects how often people drink quickly in social settings without realizing how fast their blood alcohol is rising.

## Is Blacking Out a Sign of a Drinking Problem?

Not on its own. Many social drinkers have had one or two blackouts, usually from drinking fast at an unusual event. But blackouts are worth paying attention to.

It's a good idea to talk to a doctor if:

- You black out more than once in a while
- You black out even when you're trying to pace yourself
- You drink with the aim of getting to that point
- People close to you have raised concerns about your drinking
- You've been hurt, or hurt someone else, during a blackout

A doctor's conversation about this isn't a lecture. It's a chance to look at your drinking, any medicines that might be making blackouts more likely, and practical ways to cut back if you want to.

## How to Avoid Blacking Out

The good news is that blackouts are very preventable, because they're driven mostly by speed and total amount. These habits make the biggest difference:

- **Eat a real meal before you drink**, ideally with some protein and fat, and keep snacking through the night.
- **Pace yourself.** A rough guide is about one standard drink per hour, which is close to the rate most bodies can clear.
- **Alternate with water** or another non-alcoholic drink. It slows you down without anyone noticing.
- **Skip shots and drinking games**, or limit yourself to one. They're the fastest route to a blood alcohol spike.
- **Know what's in your glass.** Cocktails, punch, and heavy pours can hold two or three standard drinks each.
- **Count your drinks.** A note on your phone works. Once you're drunk, your own estimate becomes unreliable.
- **Don't mix alcohol with sleep, anxiety, or pain medicines** unless your doctor has said it's OK.
- **Watch your drink** and don't accept drinks you didn't see poured.
- **Go out with a plan**: a set number of drinks, a time to switch to water, and a way home that doesn't involve driving.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes deeper on pacing and food, and most of it applies directly to avoiding blackouts too.

## Where DHM Fits, Honestly

People sometimes ask whether a supplement can prevent blackouts. **There is no good evidence that any supplement, DHM included, prevents blackouts in people.** Nothing you can take changes the basic math of how fast alcohol enters your blood.

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that's been studied for its effects on alcohol. A 2012 study in rats, published in the *Journal of Neuroscience*, found that DHM reduced some signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal by acting on GABA receptors. That's interesting research, but it was done in animals and hasn't been shown to protect human memory or to lower blood alcohol in a meaningful way. Human research on DHM is limited and mostly focused on how people feel the next day. Our [honest review of whether DHM works](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025) walks through what the evidence does and doesn't show.

If you're curious about DHM for next-morning symptoms on ordinary nights out, our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) and [supplement reviews](/reviews) cover the evidence and the options. It has nothing to offer for blackouts. Just don't let any supplement give you confidence to drink faster or more. It won't keep your memory switched on.

## The Bottom Line

- Being blackout drunk means your brain stopped saving new memories while you were still awake and acting.
- The main driver is a **fast rise in blood alcohol**: shots, games, chugging, and empty stomachs.
- Blackouts often happen around twice the legal driving limit, which is close to the range where alcohol poisoning becomes a risk.
- Mixing alcohol with sedating medicines makes blackouts more likely and more dangerous.
- Memory loss after very little alcohol is not normal and could mean a spiked drink or another medical problem. Get checked.
- Repeated blackouts are worth a conversation with your doctor.
- Eating first, pacing to about one drink an hour, alternating with water, and skipping shots prevent most blackouts.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does blackout drunk mean?**

Blackout drunk means you drank enough that your brain stopped saving new memories, even though you were awake, talking, and moving around. It is different from passing out, which means losing consciousness. During a blackout you can seem fairly normal to other people, but you won't remember some or all of what happened later.

**Why do I black out when I drink?**

Alcohol interferes with the hippocampus, the part of the brain that turns what is happening right now into lasting memories. The biggest driver is how fast your blood alcohol rises, not just the total amount. Drinking quickly, doing shots, drinking on an empty stomach, and mixing alcohol with sleep or anxiety medicines all make a blackout more likely. Some people also seem to be more prone to blackouts than others for reasons that are partly inherited.

**What is the difference between blacking out and passing out?**

Blacking out is a memory problem: you stay awake and can act, talk, and make decisions, but your brain isn't recording it. Passing out is a consciousness problem: you fall asleep or become unresponsive and can't be woken easily. Someone who has passed out from drinking needs to be watched closely, because the same level of alcohol can slow breathing or cause choking on vomit.

**Can you get your memories back after a blackout?**

Usually not fully. In a complete (en bloc) blackout the memories were never stored, so there is nothing to recover. In a partial blackout, sometimes called a brownout or greyout, reminders such as photos, messages, or a friend's account can bring some pieces back. Be careful with reconstructed memories, because other people's stories can fill gaps in ways that aren't accurate.

**How many drinks does it take to black out?**

There is no fixed number. Blackouts are most often linked to blood alcohol levels around 0.16% and higher, about twice the US legal driving limit, but how fast you get there matters a lot. Body size, sex, food in your stomach, and medicines all change the number. Some people black out at levels where others don't, so the only reliable way to avoid it is to drink slowly and keep the total low.

**Is blacking out a sign of a drinking problem?**

A single blackout doesn't diagnose anything, and many social drinkers have had one. But it does mean you reached a level of intoxication that carries real risk of injury and poor decisions. If blackouts happen more than once in a while, if you black out even when you try to pace yourself, or if you drink to get to that point, it's worth talking honestly with a doctor.

**Why do I black out after only a few drinks?**

Common reasons are drinking fast or on an empty stomach, strong pours or high-proof drinks, being tired or dehydrated, and mixing alcohol with medicines such as benzodiazepines, sleep aids, or some pain and anxiety medicines. If you lost memory after very little alcohol, or the memory loss doesn't fit how much you drank, consider the possibility that your drink was spiked and get medical help quickly.

**Does DHM prevent blackouts?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents blackouts in people. Early animal research found DHM reduced some signs of alcohol intoxication in rats, but that hasn't been shown to protect human memory. Some people use DHM as part of a plan to feel better the next day, but the only reliable ways to avoid a blackout are drinking less, drinking slower, and eating first.
